sheet-1.description: Sheet 1 covers the northern edge of the Rutgers College district of New Brunswick, in the large blocks between College Avenue at the top, Sicard at the middle and Wyckoff at the bottom. College Avenue is lettered 100 ft wide. Across the sheet run, from left to right, Lafayette, Huntington, Richardson, Senior and Ray, the last cut by the right edge. The blocks are numbered 91, 90, 87 and 84 above Sicard and 403, 89, 86 and 83 below it. Most of the ground is open: long lots with only a handful of frame dwellings, mostly two and two-and-a-half storeys, set along the street fronts, with a few stables and sheds behind them and one small garage marked Auto Ho. Block 84 at the upper right is entirely blank except for the compass rose. Two dwellings of hollow tile with stucco walls are marked, one on College Avenue in block 90 and one in block 87. Water mains of 6 inches run down the middle of the cross streets and 12 inches along College Avenue, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes at several corners. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that north lies towards the upper left; the grid of streets is therefore tilted on the page. Adjoining sheets named at the margins include 1A, 2A and 3A above, sheet 2 to the right, and sheet 3 below.
notes: College Avenue is lettered 100 ft wide but the blocks on either side are drawn about 60 ft apart

Sicard, Wyckoff, Lafayette, Huntington, Richardson, Senior and Ray are printed without a street suffix; modern names are Sicard Street, Wyckoff Street, Lafayette Street, Huntington Street, Richardson Street, Senior Street and Ray Street

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 lies immediately east of sheet 1 and covers the blocks between College Avenue at the top, Sicard across the middle and Wyckoff at the bottom, with Ray at the left edge and Morrell, Bartlett and Stone running down the page. Bishop Place meets College Avenue at the top near Stone. At the lower right the diagonal line of Prosper cuts across the corner, and Easton Avenue appears at the bottom right, so the last blocks on that side are drawn as wedges. Blocks 81 and 78 hold two rows of narrow attached dwellings, drawn pink for brick, set along a lane. In block 75 stands the Alpha Rho of the Chi Psi Lodge on College Avenue and, lower down, the paper box factory of P. Kalteissen, a two-storey works with stock rooms, an engine room, a coal bin, a watchman and twelve fire pails, heated and powered by steam. Block 74 contains the Lincoln School, a brick building heated by steam and lit by electricity with indirect heating, and block 80 has bowling alleys and a contractor's storage yard. Elsewhere the sheet shows frame dwellings, tenements on Wyckoff, a saloon and club buildings. The sheet is at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper left. Block 81 is blank.
notes: Sicard, Wyckoff, Ray, Morrell, Bartlett, Stone and Prosper are printed without a suffix; modern names are Sicard Street, Wyckoff Street, Ray Street, Morrell Street, Bartlett Street, Stone Street and Prosper Street
Prosper and Easton Avenue at the lower right are not used as control; Prosper meets Stone and Sicard within a few metres and its modern node is doubled

sheet-3-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 3 is the main map, the large area of the sheet outside the heavy-lined box at the lower left. It covers the district where Easton Avenue crosses a grid of streets near the centre of New Brunswick. On the right the streets run square to the page: Senior, Ray, Morrell and Bartlett cross the sheet from the Wyckoff side, with Richardson along the top edge. Easton Avenue runs diagonally through the middle of the sheet from the upper left to the lower right, and the older streets west of it, Wirt, Guilden, Delafield and Courtlandt, run at an angle to the new grid. Bristol lies at the bottom. Blocks 63, 64, 66 and 67 lie west of Easton Avenue and blocks 85, 82, 79 and 76 east of it. The most important works is the Janeway Button Co. at the corner of Courtlandt and Easton Avenue, a large brick factory with raw stock, turning, drilling and pressing rooms, an engine house and electric light, with a watchman and fire pails. Most other buildings are frame dwellings, with a bakery and flour shop and several stores along Easton Avenue, and a fire house of the Hibernia Engine Co. No. 6 in the lower right corner. The sheet is at 50 feet to an inch; north is towards the upper right.
notes: The heavy-lined box at the lower left, with its own north arrow and showing the Convent and St. Mary's Orphan Asylum, is part 2 of the sheet and was not georeferenced for lack of a street junction

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 covers the blocks along Central Avenue and the streets south of it, in the south-western part of the old city. Central Avenue crosses the sheet from the upper left to the lower right as a very wide street whose left side is blank, and most of the left half of the sheet is empty. The drawn blocks lie in two groups. At the top, around Duke, Courtlandt and Delafield, blocks 62, 65 and 408 hold frame dwellings and one triangular island of land between Central Avenue and Courtlandt. In the lower right, Robinson and Hartwell run south from Central Avenue to Hamilton at the bottom of the sheet, with blocks 59 and 58 on either side. Block 58 includes the premises of F. G. Robinson, specialties in knit goods, stoves and kerosene, with a knitting room and office. The buildings are almost all two-storey frame dwellings on narrow lots, with a few pink brick houses. Water mains of 4, 6 and 8 inches are shown in the streets. The sheet is at 50 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper right. Sheets 3 and 5 adjoin on the right and sheet 9 is below.
notes: Central Avenue is not used as control because its drawn width and outline differ from the modern street; one junction on it carried a residual over 3 m

sheet-5-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 5 is the main map, covering the area outside the heavy-lined box at the lower left. It lies on the south side of Central Avenue and shows the point where Central Avenue, Delafield, Prosper and Mine meet the older diagonal streets. The upper right has two long blocks, 68 and 69, between Delafield and Guilden and east of Guilden, bounded at the top by Bristol and at the bottom by Prosper. Block 69 contains a school building marked not in use, and block 68 a Hungarian chapel heated by stoves and lit by electricity. South of Prosper, block 70 holds shops along Easton Avenue including a bakery, a hardware and paint store and the works of the Pen-Carbon Manifold Co., which has an engine, a boiler and a watchman and is heated by steam. Block 56 on Mine and Easton Avenue is mostly frame dwellings. At the left a long wedge, block 57, lies between Hartwell, Central Avenue and Hamilton, with narrow lots running back from Hamilton and dwellings facing Hartwell. High Street and Division Street meet Hamilton at the bottom. The sheet is at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that north lies towards the upper right. The adjoining sheet numbers 2, 3, 4 and 6 appear at the margins.
notes: Part 2 of the sheet, the heavy-lined box at the lower left, was anchored on one point and is low confidence

sheet-5-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 5 is the boxed area at the lower left corner of the sheet, bounded by a heavy double line and drawn with its own north arrow. It shows a short stretch of Hamilton, which crosses the box from the upper left to the lower right, with Hardenbergh and Guilden entering from the left edge and Easton Avenue running down the right side of the box. Blocks 5 and 56 lie north of Hamilton and block 11 south of it, the last almost blank. Only a few buildings are drawn: a row of dwellings along the left side near Guilden, a frame house on the corner of Easton Avenue and Hamilton, an auto garage, and two small outbuildings. The rest of the box is open lots and vacant ground. Water mains of 8 inches run in Hamilton and 10 inches in Easton Avenue. The part is drawn at the same scale as the main map, 50 feet to an inch, and has a north arrow pointing to the upper right. It repeats ground that the main map also shows, so its position was fixed from a single hand-picked junction, Guilden, Hamilton and Hardenbergh, at the left edge.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 covers the Rutgers College district north-west of the college grounds. Prosper and Mine run across the upper left as diagonal streets, and Union runs down the middle from Mine to Hamilton, which closes the sheet at the bottom. Easton Avenue crosses the left side, and College Avenue, lettered as a wide street, forms the right-hand edge. Stone is at the top. Blocks 71, 55 and 54 and the rows of lots along College Avenue are drawn, including a building lettered Fraternity Ho. on the right. The built-up ground is chiefly large frame dwellings set in generous lots, with a small brick building on Mine; St. James M. E. Church and its parsonage stand on the lower left block facing Hamilton, heated by steam and lit by electricity. At the lower right the Van Doren and Merres mineral refinery occupies a large works with gas engines, bottling and grinding rooms and a bin, powered by gas engine and heated by stoves and steam, the boiler and engine not used. Water mains of 6, 8 and 12 inches are shown. The sheet is at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper right. Neighbouring sheets 2, 5, 7 and 11 are named at the margins.
notes: Stone, Prosper, Mine, Union and Hamilton are printed without a suffix; modern names are Stone Street, Prosper Street, Mine Street, Union Street and Hamilton Street

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 shows the main Rutgers College and New Brunswick Theological Seminary grounds, drawn at 60 feet to an inch, not 50. College Avenue runs down the left side and George along the right, the latter bending near the middle. Bishop Place crosses the top and Seminary Place the middle of the sheet, with Hamilton closing the bottom. In the upper block stands the Theological Seminary of the Reformed Church in America, with Gardner A. Sage Library, Peter Hertzog Hall, a dormitory, and James Suydam Hall with its gymnasium, class rooms and a stage, together with dwellings lettered A to F and the Chi Phi house. Along Bishop Place several lots are drawn with frame dwellings. Below Seminary Place lie two college blocks separated by Bleeker Place. In the western one are the State Experiment Station with N. J. Hall and the Entomological Laboratory, a greenhouse and the Delta Phi house; in the eastern one stand the Chemistry Building, the Engineering Building, the Scarlet Club, Delta Upsilon, the Ralph Voorhees Library and the Robt. F. Ballantine Gymnasium, all of Rutgers College. The sheet is drawn with north towards the upper right.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 covers the industrial riverside north-east of the college district in New Brunswick, between the Delaware and Raritan Canal and its feeder at the top and Somerset Street at the bottom. Hamilton Street crosses the sheet from the left edge, with George Street running down the left margin. Most of the sheet belongs to the Johnson and Johnson works, shown in pink as numbered brick buildings: a large block above Hamilton between the canal lock and George Street, a second range on the east side of the canal feeder beside George Street, where a heavy line runs along the street and turns east, and the former Norfolk and New Brunswick Hosiery Company mill and the Neverslip Manufacturing Company below Hamilton. Iron bridges carry the works across the canal arms. Neilson Street runs down the middle of the lower half past the Pennsylvania Railroad, whose multiple tracks, retaining walls and a bridged crossing cut diagonally from lower left to the right edge. East of Water Street stand the Consolidated Fruit Jar Company, the New Jersey Lamp and Bronze Works, with a printed note on their sprinkler and fire protection, and a line of small frame dwellings fronting Somerset Street at the bottom. The Raritan River and a canal basin close the right edge. A compass and a second north arrow lie near the right margin, and the sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Only one junction, Hamilton Street with George Street, is drawn with a measurable water-pipe crossing at the left edge of the sheet; the part is placed from that point and is low confidence

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 shows a thinly built part of the north-western college district of New Brunswick, bounded by Hamilton Street along the top, Somerset Street along the bottom, Louis Street on the left and Plum Street at the right edge. Harvey Street runs through the middle of the sheet, bending at the top where it is lettered Robinson Street north of Hamilton, and Hartwell Street continues Plum Street north of Hamilton. Most of the area is large open blocks, numbered 52A, 52C and 52D, with few buildings. Frame dwellings line Hamilton Street and the west side of Louis Street, and the left edge has the glasshouses of Geo. H. Bond, florist. Near the top centre, beside Robinson Street, stands the Rutgers College Preparatory School with its dormitory. A long iron clad warehouse and the main factory of the United Cigar Manufacturing Company, New Brunswick Branch, occupy the lower middle of the sheet, with a printed note on its sprinklers and fire fighting equipment. St. Ladislaus Hungarian Catholic Church and a Hungarian Lutheran church lie east of the factory near Plum Street, and a row of dwellings front Plum Street. Water pipes of six to twelve inches run down each street. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper right.
notes: Robinson Street north of Hamilton Street is the northern continuation of Harvey Street, jogged about 15 m; the north-branch control point uses the modern Robinson Street node
Hartwell Street north of Hamilton Street is the northern branch of Plum Street, jogged about 6 m; the control point uses the modern Hartwell Street node
Hamilton Street junctions are placed from water-pipe crossings because the north edge of Hamilton Street is not drawn as a street line

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 covers the residential blocks of New Brunswick between Hamilton Street, which slants across the top of the sheet, and Somerset Street along the bottom. Four streets run down the sheet: Plum Street at the left, then High Street, Division Street and Hardenbergh Street at the right, where Condict Street opens at the edge. Hartwell Street, the northern branch of Plum Street, and Guilden Street enter from Hamilton Street at the top. The blocks, numbered 52 and 51, are filled with narrow lots carrying frame dwellings, mostly two and a half storeys, with sheds, and stores at some corners. In the lower middle the Memorial Baptist Chapel stands on High Street, Mt. Zion A.M.E. Church lies beside Division Street, and St. Peter's Parochial School and St. Peter's Hospital, with its laundry and engine room, occupy the south-east block near Hardenbergh Street. Along the bottom edge Scott Street runs south from Somerset Street and Albany Street opens at the lower right, with the neighbouring sheets 16, 17 and 11 numbered there. The streets are drawn about 50 to 60 feet wide with water pipes down the centres. A compass in the upper right shows north towards the upper right, and the sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Hartwell Street north of Hamilton Street is the northern branch of Plum Street, jogged about 6 m; its control point is a water-pipe crossing and sits about 8 m from the fit of the detected points, so the upper left corner is less certain
Guilden Street, Hamilton Street and Hardenbergh Street meet at one junction near the right edge
Plum, High, Division, Hardenbergh between Hamilton and Somerset; St. Peter's hospital and school. The helper's hand-picked Hamilton / Hartwell point (8 m off the detected points) was dropped.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 shows the blocks of New Brunswick between Hamilton Street at the top and the Pennsylvania Railroad at the bottom right, around the diagonal line of Easton Avenue. Hardenbergh Street runs down the left side, where it meets Condict Street and then Somerset Street, and College Avenue forms the right edge. Easton Avenue crosses the sheet from the upper left to the lower right and divides the blocks into wedges; Condict Street and Somerset Street cross it at the middle, Albany and French Streets run across the lower half, and Brown Street runs down the lower left. The blocks, numbered 47 to 50, are filled with frame dwellings on narrow lots, with stores and shops along Easton Avenue. In the upper centre F. E. Watson and Company's water colour works stand near Condict Street. A large livery stable with carriages and furniture storage, in blue, lies on the north-east side of Easton Avenue, with a ceramic department, an undertaker's and several shops beside it. The Rutgers Preparatory School, with the Zeta Psi house, the Annex and the Queens Club, stands near the College Avenue edge at the upper right. The Pennsylvania Railroad, with retaining walls, cuts across the bottom right. The compass shows north towards the upper right, and the sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Brown Street, at the lower left, is not in today's street network
The Easton Avenue and Somerset Street junction carries a residual of about 3 m, probably because Easton Avenue is drawn wider than today's
Easton Avenue wedges between Hardenbergh and College Avenue; Condict, Somerset, Albany, French; one part.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 covers the Rutgers College campus and the New Brunswick passenger station district. College Avenue runs down the left side, Hamilton Street crosses the top, and George Street forms the right edge, with Somerset Street crossing the sheet below the campus. The campus, lettered Rutgers College and Campus, fills the large block in the upper middle and carries Van Nest Hall, Geological Hall, the Queens Building, the Sophia Kirkpatrick Memorial Chapel, the Club House and Winants Hall with its dining rooms and dormitory, and at the upper right the Daniel S. Schanck Observatory. Below Somerset Street lie St. Peter's Roman Catholic Church with its convent and rectory, a block of shops and dwellings, and the Fire Department Protection Engine Company No. 5. Easton Avenue runs along the lower left past Washington Street. The Pennsylvania Railroad crosses the lower half diagonally, with its stone retaining walls, a tunnel, and the passenger station and its sheds at the lower middle. East of the tracks, Washington Street and Albany Street border a block of stores, a tailor shop, a drug store and the German Reformed Church along George Street. The compass at the left shows north towards the upper right, and the sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Somerset Street east of George Street is drawn about 1000 pixels (125 ft) south of the west part; the control point is the junction west of George Street
The Pennsylvania Railroad is the present Northeast Corridor
The Somerset Street and Wall Street, Easton Avenue and Wall Street, Albany Street and Easton Avenue and Albany Street and Washington Street junctions were not detected
Rutgers campus, station and Pennsylvania Railroad between College Avenue and George Street; one part.

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 shows the manufacturing and tenement district of New Brunswick between the Delaware and Raritan Canal at the top, George Street along the bottom, Somerset Street at the left and Albany Street along the right, drawn turned so that north lies towards the upper left. Water, Peace, Catharine and Neilson Streets cross the sheet from the Albany Street side, and Washington Street runs down the middle. The upper part holds the Janeway and Company wall paper factory by the canal, the Public Service gas works with its holders and generator house, the large India Rubber Company mill, and, to the right of Water Street, the Endurance Tire and Rubber Company, the New Brunswick Iron Works, the L. T. Ives needle works, J. D. Watson and Company's colour works, W. Schlesinger's coal, hay and grain yard, and the Bell Hotel and White Hall Hotel. Below them the blocks are filled with frame tenements, shops and stables, with the Albany Hotel, a Jewish church and the Mansion House along Albany Street, and, near the bottom left, the Middlesex Shoe Company factory on City Alley. Marsh Alley and an unnamed alley cross the lower blocks. Printed notes list the sprinkler and watchman systems of the larger works. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Most streets drawn here (Water, Peace, Catharine, Washington, Neilson, Somerset) were removed or realigned by the Route 18 and urban renewal works and are not in today's street network
Only the Albany Street and Neilson Street junction could be measured; the part is anchored on it with the atlas scale and is low confidence
The Albany Street and George Street junction lies about 46 ft below the bottom edge of the sheet
Janeway, gas works and India Rubber district by the canal, turned about -60 degrees; anchored on Albany / Neilson, low confidence (Water, Peace, Catharine, Washington gone: Route 18).

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 covers two rows of city blocks on the north-western edge of New Brunswick, drawn with north towards the upper right. Jersey Avenue runs across the sheet from left to right and divides an upper row of blocks (numbered 224, 223, 204 and 203) from a lower row (225, 222, 205 and 202). The cross streets are, from left to right, Sandford, Delavan, Comstock, Hale and Baldwin, and French Street runs diagonally across the top of the upper blocks, where the sheet is cut by its edge, with Oxford Street branching from it at the upper right. The upper blocks are long, narrow and lined with frame dwellings, sheds and a few stables, with large vacant stretches at their lower ends. The Union Athletic Club, a brick building, stands in block 203 beside a marble works. In the lower row the most prominent works are Rolfe's Lumber Yard, with its lumber sheds, piles and drive-ways, and C. W. Russell's coal and grain business with a grain elevator and coal pockets. The lower part of the sheet is taken by the Pennsylvania Railroad, with a long P.R.R. freight shed, a platform, a spur into the lumber yard and a wide fan of running tracks and yard tracks. A base ball park is named in the open ground at the top right. Six-inch and twelve-inch water pipes run along the streets, and the street widths of 60 and 80 feet are lettered beside them. Sheets 54 and 53 adjoin on the left, sheet 15 on the right and sheet 22 below.
notes: The Pennsylvania Railroad tracks at the bottom of the sheet lie about 25 m from the modern Northeast Corridor line; they were not used as control.
Oxford Street / French Street was left out of the fit because its modern junction sits about 3 m off the drawn one.
Reading made from the 1600 px overview, not from 1:1 crops.
Jersey Avenue blocks between Sandford and Baldwin, French / Oxford at top, P.R.R. yard at bottom; Oxford Street left out (3 m off).

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15 shows the blocks on either side of Jersey Avenue in the north-west of New Brunswick, drawn with north towards the upper right. The upper half is a fan of narrow blocks (numbered 99, 98, 97 and 96) between Oxford, Bethany, Alexander, James and Louis Streets, which run down to French Street; Somerset Street bounds them along the top. Block 184, a vacant wedge, lies at the left beside the compass. Below Jersey Avenue the blocks 185, 183 and 165 lie between Baldwin, Handy, Seaman and Suydam Streets, with Railroad Avenue at the bottom edge beside the Pennsylvania Railroad. Most lots hold frame dwellings with sheds. The industries are the Kilburn Manufacturing Corporation, makers of knitting machines, at the top of block 98; Wm. Rust and Son Co., makers of poultry remedies, beside a junk yard in block 99; the Morrison Blue Co. and L. S. Perkins, rubber specialties, at the foot of Bethany Street; Swift and Co., refrigerator and shipping, in block 185 with a railroad spur; W. T. McAdams, wholesale grocer; and Armour and Co., refrigerator, near the bottom. The Washington School, brick and heated by steam, stands at the corner of French and Louis Streets. Water pipes of 4, 6, 8, 12 and 16 inches run along the streets. Sheet 14 adjoins on the left, sheet 16 on the right, sheet 9 above and sheet 23 below.
notes: Seaman Street and James Street, and Suydam Street and Louis Street, are drawn as one line each either side of French Street; OpenStreetMap has two nodes about 5 to 10 m apart for each pair.
Reading made from the 1600 px overview, not from 1:1 crops.
Oxford to Louis fan above Jersey Avenue, Baldwin to Suydam below; one part.

sheet-16.description: Sheet 16 shows the district between Somerset Street and French Street in the north-west of New Brunswick, drawn with north towards the upper left, so that French Street runs up the middle of the page. To the left of French lie four long blocks, numbered 27, 28, 29 and 30 from the top, between Scott, Plum, Prospect, Harvey and Louis Streets, with Somerset Street along the left edge. They hold mostly frame dwellings, some in tight rows of two-and-a-half storey houses along Plum Street, together with a hotel and a bakery with ovens near French Street, a furniture and spring-bed works (F. J. Potter and Co.), a blacksmith and a plumbing shop. To the right of French the sheet shows block 17, a large empty wedge between Paterson, Bayard and New Streets that belongs to sheet 17 and is drawn only in outline, and blocks 145 and 164 below it, between Townsend and Suydam Streets, which carry small dwellings and sheds. Railroad Avenue and the Pennsylvania Railroad lie along the right edge. Water pipes of 4, 6, 8 and 12 inches run along the streets and the lettered widths are 40, 60 and 80 feet. The compass rose stands in the empty block 17. Sheets 9 and 10 adjoin on the left, sheet 17 above and to the right, sheets 24 and 23 on the right edge and sheet 15 below.
notes: Louis Street and Suydam Street are one line either side of French Street; OpenStreetMap has two nodes about 10 m apart.
Harvey Street and Townsend Street are one line offset about 12 m at French Street.
Block 17 is drawn here as an empty outline; its content is on sheet 17.
Reading made from the 1600 px overview, not from 1:1 crops.
Somerset to French, Scott to Louis, plus Townsend / Suydam; one part.

sheet-17-1.description: Part 1 is the main map of sheet 17, drawn with north towards the top and slightly to the right, and covers the part of New Brunswick where the Pennsylvania Railroad crosses the streets north of the station. At the top, Somerset Street runs along the upper left, and French Street crosses the sheet diagonally from the left to the right edge, with Scott Street coming down from the upper left to meet it. Block 26, between Scott and Brown Streets, is taken by two institutions: the Children's Industrial Home, with kitchen, dining room and new wing, and the Wells Memorial Hospital, a cross-shaped building with women's and men's wards, kitchen and operating room, together with a band hall and studios. French Street is lined with dwellings, a bowling alley and the Middlesex Transportation Co. express building, and at the right with C. W. Russell's coal and grain sheds. The Pennsylvania Railroad crosses the page from lower left to upper right as a band of six tracks. Below French lie Paterson Street, with the Hadkins Bottling Co., a sausage works and an auto house, and Bayard Street, and below them the long wedge of New Street and Railroad Avenue with rows of dwellings and a milk depot. The Magyar Church stands at the right edge beside Schuyler Street. An inset drawn in a heavy outline at the left is part 2. Water pipes of 6 and 8 inches run along the streets. Sheets 10, 11 and 16 adjoin above and on the left, sheets 24 and 18 below and to the right.
notes: Schuyler Street is today Joyce Kilmer Avenue North; the part is placed from its junction with Paterson Street.

Placed from one measured junction at the atlas scale: Scott Street, French Street and Paterson Street meet in a cluster that the detector could not read, and the junctions at the right edge on French and Bayard Streets disagreed with it by 5 to 6 m.
Reading made from the 1600 px overview, not from 1:1 crops.

Two parts: 1 main (Albany to New, Division to Schuyler), anchored on Joyce Kilmer Avenue North / Paterson (low confidence); 2 inset block 25 at French and Bayard, anchored on a point carried from sheet 16 (low confidence).

sheet-17-2.description: Part 2 is a small inset at the left of sheet 17, drawn in a heavy outline with its own north arrow, and shows a single block, numbered 25, between French Street and Bayard Street. The block is a long wedge lying along the diagonal French Street at its upper left and along Bayard Street at its foot. A frame dwelling with a rear shed stands at its tip, a small outbuilding near it, and a one-storey building with a yard stands at its far end. The rest of the block is vacant. The inset has been drawn here to show a piece of ground that falls on the empty block of sheet 16, and New Street is named below Bayard Street. Water pipes of 8 inches run along both streets. The surrounding spaces inside the outline are marked with the numbers of the adjoining sheets 16 and 17.
notes: Placed from one corner, the tip of block 25, carried from the matching outline of the empty block on sheet 16; scale is the atlas scale and rotation was set from the French Street edge. Low confidence.
Reading made from the 1600 px overview, not from 1:1 crops.

Two parts: 1 main (Albany to New, Division to Schuyler), anchored on Joyce Kilmer Avenue North / Paterson (low confidence); 2 inset block 25 at French and Bayard, anchored on a point carried from sheet 16 (low confidence).

sheet-18-1.description: Part 1 is the main map of sheet 18 and shows the centre of New Brunswick around the county buildings, drawn with north towards the top and slightly to the right. Church Street runs across the upper part and Paterson Street and Bayard Street across the middle and lower part, crossed by Schuyler Street at the left, Kirkpatrick Street in the centre and Spring Street, which becomes Elm Row, at the right. At the top, French Street runs diagonally past the Pennsylvania Railroad, whose tracks cross the upper left corner, and the sheet shows the Hygeni Milk Co., the Imperial Cigar Factory, express offices, saloons, a paint shop, and a long block of dwellings along Church Street containing the New Brunswick Garage and a livery stable. The block between Paterson and Bayard Streets is the county seat: the County Jail with cells, the County Court House, heated by steam and lit by electricity, and the County Offices stand in a large open lot. Dwellings fill the blocks to the left and below. A heavy outline at the lower right encloses a separate inset, part 2, of the Brookford Snuff Mill on Lawrence Brook, which is not georeferenced. Water pipes of 4, 6 and 8 inches are lettered along the streets. Sheets 11 and 12 adjoin above, 17 on the left, 19 on the right, 24 and 25 below.
notes: Schuyler Street is today Joyce Kilmer Avenue North.
Church Street / Spring Street was not detected and is not in the fit.
Reading made from the 1600 px overview, not from 1:1 crops.
Two parts: 1 main downtown, county buildings, Schuyler (Joyce Kilmer Avenue North) to George; 2 inset Brookford Snuff Mill (J. M. Parsons) on Lawrence Brook, 3 1/2 miles south, unplaced.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Brookford Snuff Mill (J. M. Parsons) on Lawrence Brook, 3 1/2 miles south of the court house (no street junction; needs a located position for the mill).

sheet-19.description: Sheet 19 shows the commercial centre of New Brunswick, in a grid of city blocks drawn with north towards the top and slightly to the right. Albany Street runs across the top, followed by Church, Paterson and Bayard Streets, crossed by Spring Street and Elm Row at the left, George Street in the middle and Neilson Street at the right. The blocks are mostly densely built with brick stores and offices heated by steam: the Post Office, a fireproof building, the National Bank Building, a department store and the Telephone Exchange at the top left; a large cigar factory and the Elk's building; the Second Reformed Church with its chapel, the Williamson Garage, the Public Service office and a motion picture house and open air theatre at the top right; and the New Brunswick Fire Insurance Co.'s building, the New Brunswick Trust Co. and the First Baptist Church in the lower left. A block between Church and Paterson Streets holds a bank, a business college, a restaurant and a large department store at the left. On the right of George Street the blocks between Church and Paterson and between Paterson and Bayard Streets are taken by cemetery grounds, with Christ Church Episcopal, the Old and New Parish Houses, the First Presbyterian Church, the First Reformed Church and its chapel. Water pipes of 4, 6, 8 and 12 inches run in all the streets. Neighbouring sheets are 12 and 13 above, 18 and 20 on either side, and 25 and 26 below.
notes: Neilson Street is drawn about 42 ft wide against about 70 ft in today's parcels; street_widths was set to 42.
Hiram Street at the right edge is not in the OpenStreetMap extract under that name.
Reading made from the 1600 px overview, not from 1:1 crops.
Downtown commercial centre, Albany to Bayard, Spring / Elm Row to Neilson; Neilson drawn 42 ft (street_widths); one part.

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 covers part of the downtown commercial district of New Brunswick, from Albany Street at the top of the sheet to Richmond Street at the bottom, and from Neilson Street on the left to the Delaware and Raritan Canal and the Raritan River frontage on the right. Church, Hiram and Richmond Streets cross the sheet east and west, and Dennis Street, Neilson Street, Peace Street and Burnet Street run across it from top to bottom, with Little Burnet Street a narrow way beside Burnet on the right. The left half of the sheet is a dense grid of three-storey brick stores, hotels and lodging houses with frame dwellings behind. Named buildings include the Milton Hotel, the Raritan House, Stout's Building, the King Block, the New Brunswick Daily Times, the Home News, a motion picture theatre, McDede's garage, J. H. Weigel Jr. Hardware Company, an athletic club, the Hotel Neilson, a bottling works, the Peoples Mission, the Salvation Army, a synagogue and the Crawford Manufacturing Company with the New Brunswick Needle Works. Phoenix Engine Company No. 3 stands at the lower left, with its equipment described in a note at the foot of the sheet. The right half is industrial: the large United States Rubber Company works and its annex, with sprinklered mill buildings, and below them the Raritan Coal Company, a lumber company, W. S. Strong hardware, a lumber yard, Tindel's coal yard, the Welch coal yard and a lime works, all backing on the canal. A note on watchmen and fire protection and a compass rose are at the upper right. Scale is 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Burnet Street was rebuilt as part of Route 18 and the modern Burnet Street junctions with Albany Street and Richmond Street lie 10 to 40 m from the drawn ones; they were not used as control.
Peace Street, Little Burnet Street and the riverside blocks east of Burnet Street no longer exist.
The modern node where Dennis Street meets Hiram Square lies about 7 m from the drawn junction and was not used.
Neilson Street is drawn about 40 feet wide, narrower than its modern right-of-way.
Downtown blocks Albany to Richmond, Neilson to the canal; Burnet Street left out (Route 18, 9 to 37 m off); weak control along Neilson, low confidence.

sheet-21.description: Sheet 21 shows an outlying residential part of New Brunswick in the south-west of the city, between the Pennsylvania Railroad along the top edge of the sheet and Livingston Avenue along the bottom. Codwise Avenue crosses the middle of the sheet, and the cross streets from left to right are Ward, Talmadge, Howard and Powers, with Sandford Street at the right edge; Ward Street is cut by the left edge. Each street is lettered as 60 feet wide. Eight long blocks, numbered 265, 260, 246 and 241 north of Codwise Avenue and 266, 259, 247 and 240 south of it, are almost entirely open lots divided by faint lot lines, with a scatter of two-storey frame dwellings, sheds and a few outbuildings along the street frontages. The only industrial buildings are the Prospect Boiler Shop, a brick works with night watchman and steam power, in block 246, and a lumber storage shed, a carpenter shop and the Cue Tip Manufacturing Company on the right side of block 241. A boarding house stands at the foot of block 246. Water pipes of six and eight inches run down the middle of the streets. Fire alarm and telephone boxes stand at several corners. A compass rose is placed in block 260 with north towards the upper right. Adjoining sheets are 53 above, 23 to the left, 22 to the right and 27 below. Scale is 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Codwise Avenue is today Joyce Kilmer Avenue.
The sheet's Talmadge Street is Llewellyn Place and Columbus Place in OpenStreetMap north of Livingston Avenue; Howard Street meets Joyce Kilmer Avenue at a node named Stratford Place.
Railroad Avenue is not drawn on this sheet; the Pennsylvania Railroad is shown by a strip at the top edge.
Codwise (Joyce Kilmer) Avenue to Livingston Avenue, Ward to Sandford; Talmadge = Llewellyn / Columbus Place, Howard = Stratford Place at Codwise.

sheet-22.description: Sheet 22 lies in the south-western outskirts of New Brunswick and continues sheet 21 to the east. Railroad Avenue and the Pennsylvania Railroad form the top edge, Codwise Avenue crosses the middle and Livingston Avenue runs along the bottom. The cross streets from left to right are Sandford at the left edge, then Delavan, Comstock, Hale and Baldwin at the right edge; the name Hale is struck through on the sheet. Streets are lettered 60 or 80 feet wide, with water pipes of four, six, eight and sixteen inches down their centres. The blocks are long and thinly built. Block 221, north of Codwise Avenue between Delavan and Comstock, is a large open tract lettered Play Grounds. Blocks 226, 206 and 201 are mostly vacant, with a few dwellings and a summer house on 226 and a short row of dwellings on the south side of 201. South of Codwise Avenue, blocks 220 and 207 and the blocks beside them carry frame dwellings with rear sheds; S. M. Starkey's bottling works, with a gasoline engine and storage, stands on block 207, and a livery and an auto house are drawn in the lower blocks. Block 200 at the right edge has a row of two-storey dwellings along Codwise Avenue and a stable. A compass rose is in block 221. The adjoining sheets are 14 above, 21 to the left, 23 to the right and 27 and 28 below. Scale is 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Codwise Avenue is today Joyce Kilmer Avenue.
Hale Street is struck through on the sheet; it appears as Hale Street in OpenStreetMap.
Railroad Avenue has a carriageway on each side of the railroad in OpenStreetMap and was not used as control on this sheet.
Sandford to Baldwin, Railroad Avenue to Livingston Avenue; one part.

sheet-23.description: Sheet 23 covers four and a half residential blocks in the south-western part of New Brunswick, between Railroad Avenue along the Pennsylvania Railroad at the top of the sheet and Livingston Avenue at the bottom, with Codwise Avenue crossing the middle. The cross streets are, from left to right, Baldwin, Handy, Seaman, Suydam and Townsend, the last cut by the right edge of the sheet. Drift street runs diagonally from the corner of Handy and Codwise Avenue down to Suydam, cutting the blocks south of Codwise into wedges. Blocks 186, 182, 166 and 163 lie north of Codwise Avenue and blocks 187, 181, 167, 168, 162 and 161 south of it. The area is almost entirely frame dwellings, mostly two storeys, set on narrow lots with stables and sheds behind; a few stores stand at corners. The Suydam Street Reformed Church, a brick building heated by furnace and lit by electricity, stands on the corner of Suydam and Drift, with a carpenter's shop nearby. P. H. Hendricks, contractor and builder, has a yard with sheds in block 182 off Handy. Six-inch water pipes run down the middle of each street, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes at several corners. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper right (about 51 degrees clockwise from the top), the street grid running square to the page. Adjoining sheets are 15 and 16 above, 22 to the left, 24 to the right and 28 and 29 below.
notes: Codwise Avenue is today Joyce Kilmer Avenue.
Railroad Avenue has a carriageway on each side of the railroad in OpenStreetMap; the sheet draws the south side.
Railroad Avenue to Livingston Avenue, Baldwin to Townsend; Codwise Avenue (today Joyce Kilmer Avenue) across the middle. One part; pilot sheet (default detector settings).

sheet-24.description: Sheet 24 shows the area where the street grid of south-western New Brunswick meets the diagonal New Street. Railroad Avenue and the Pennsylvania Railroad cross the top left, Codwise Avenue runs across the middle and Livingston Avenue along the bottom. Townsend Street is cut by the left edge and Redmond and Welton Streets cross the sheet from top to bottom. Drift Street runs obliquely across the lower left, cutting the blocks into wedges, and New Street runs from the top right to the lower right as a wide diagonal, met by Schuyler Street, Kirkpatrick Street and, at the top, Bayard Street. The blocks are numbered 146, 144, 147, 148, 143, 142, 131 and 130. Development is mostly frame dwellings of two and two and a half storeys with stables, set along the street frontages, with rows of narrow lots on the Codwise Avenue side of block 144. Institutional and commercial buildings include the Livingston School in block 142, Neptune Engine Company No. 2, a fire department building with its equipment listed on the sheet, W. H. Vansickle Jr., contractor, a contractors' yard and lime house on Railroad Avenue, the New Brunswick Storage Warehouse Company, a livery and the Livingston Apartments. A large area east of New Street is blank. A compass rose is at the right. Scale is 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Codwise Avenue is today Joyce Kilmer Avenue.
The street lettered New may be lettered New Street; the suffix is not legible where it is cut off by the diagonal.
Railroad Avenue was left out of the control because its junctions are 5 m off and the railroad runs in the street.
Redmond, Welton, Drift, New Street area between Railroad and Livingston Avenues; Railroad Avenue left out (rail in street).

sheet-25.description: Sheet 25 shows the diagonal crossing of Livingston Avenue and New Street, at the south-western edge of the central part of New Brunswick. Bayard Street runs along the top edge with Kirkpatrick Street at the left, Elm Row in the upper middle and George Street at the right. Livingston Avenue crosses the sheet diagonally from lower left to upper right, and New Street, Carroll Place, Schureman Street and Morris Street cut across the lower half. Drift Street enters from the left edge. Block 12 at the top is large, with dwellings along Bayard Street and Kirkpatrick Street and the Evangelical Lutheran Emanuel Church at its lower left corner, a brick building with a tower, heated by furnace and lit by electricity. Block 127 is a small triangular lot, block 128 holds frame dwellings, a boarding house and a lodging house, and block 129 at the bottom holds the Grand Army of the Republic hall, the Bolkert Flats, a livery and a carriage house, an undertaker and a number of two-storey dwellings along Morris Street. A cigar and candy shop, a Chinese laundry and rows of dwellings are on George Street. Water pipes run in all streets, with sizes from four to twenty inches. A compass rose is at the left. The neighbouring sheets are 18, 19, 24, 26, 30 and 34. Scale is 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Schureman Street and Carroll Place are not in OpenStreetMap.
The modern node where Livingston Avenue and Liberty Street meet George Street is one point; the drawn junctions of the two streets with George Street are about 11 m apart.
Bayard to Morris, Kirkpatrick to George; Livingston Avenue diagonal; one part.

sheet-26.description: Sheet 26 covers the blocks south of Bayard Street in central New Brunswick, between George Street on the left and Neilson Street on the right. Bayard Street runs along the top, Liberty Street, Schureman Street, Carroll Place, New Street and Morris Street cross from left to right at intervals down the sheet, and Richmond Street meets Neilson Street at the right. Livingston Avenue enters at the left. The map area is drawn between x positions about a fifth in from the left edge and the right edge; the left margin carries printed notes on Fire Department Hose Company No. 1 and Truck Company No. 1. Block 8, at the top, holds the Bayard Street School, a Knights of Columbus club with a lodge room, the Bijou M. P. Theatre, a carriage store house, the Webb Wire Works and rows of dwellings. Block 117 holds the First Methodist Episcopal Church, the Opera House, the City Water Works and its supply shed, a police station and the fire department building of the Liberty Fire Station. Block 118 is a long block of two-storey dwellings and stores, with a furniture and furnace repair shop at the right end. Block 119 at the bottom holds dwellings, sheds and a carriage house. Water pipes run in all streets. A compass rose is at the right. Adjoining sheets are 19, 20, 25, 34 and 35. Scale is 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Schureman Street and Carroll Place are not in OpenStreetMap.
The Liberty Fire Station and the Opera House stood on Liberty Street.
Bayard to Morris between George and Neilson; left margin (fire department notes) masked.

sheet-27.description: Sheet 27 covers eight blocks of the south-western part of New Brunswick in two rows of four. Livingston Avenue runs along the top of the sheet, Lee Avenue crosses the middle and Remsen Avenue closes the bottom. The cross streets are, from left to right, Talmadge, Howard, Powers, Sandford and Delavan, the last two cut by the right edge. Blocks 258, 248, 239 and 228 lie north of Lee Avenue and blocks 257, 249, 238 and 229 south of it. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 51 degrees from north, so that the streets run square to the page, and the compass rose at the upper right puts north towards the top right corner. Most of the area is thinly built: the long blocks hold scattered frame dwellings with stables and sheds, and several blocks, notably 248, 239, 238 and 229, are largely empty lots divided by property lines. A single industrial plant stands in block 249, the New Brunswick Iron and Metal Company, with two stores for rags and paper along a narrow lot, with a scales house at the foot of the lot; it is marked with no watchman, no clock, no power and no fire apparatus. Two dwellings with concrete block walls are shown in blocks 239 and 228, and a carpenter shop in 239. Six-inch water pipes run down the middle of each street, with a twelve-inch main under Livingston Avenue and an eight-inch main under Remsen Avenue, and hydrants and fire alarm boxes stand at several corners. The adjoining sheets are 21 and 22 above, 28 to the right and 31 below.
notes: North lies towards the upper right of the page; the fitted rotation of the sheet is about 51 degrees.
Delavan Street is cut by the right edge of the sheet and is only partly drawn.
Livingston, Lee and Remsen Avenues, Talmadge to Delavan; thinly built; one part.

sheet-28.description: Sheet 28 shows eight blocks east of sheet 27, in two rows of four, between Livingston Avenue at the top, Lee Avenue across the middle and Remsen Avenue at the bottom. From left to right the cross streets are Delavan, Comstock, Hale, Baldwin and Handy, the first and last on the edges of the sheet. North of Lee Avenue are blocks 219, 208, 199 and 188, and south of it blocks 218, 209, 198 and 189. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, with the street grid turned about 51 degrees from north; the large compass rose stands in the empty block 219 at upper left. Livingston Avenue, Lee Avenue and the cross streets are lettered 60 feet wide. The area is a mixed residential district: frame dwellings of two and two and a half storeys line the street fronts, with tenements on Baldwin Street, rows of attached dwellings in block 188 near Lee Avenue. The Ebenezer Baptist Church, heated by furnace and lit by electricity, stands at the corner of Comstock and Lee in block 209. A greenhouse, heated by steam, fills a long lot in block 208, with a bowling alley beside it, and a store and an office stand on Hale Street. Two ruined buildings appear in block 218. Water pipes of four and six inches run in the streets and a twelve-inch main under Livingston Avenue. Adjoining sheets are 22 and 23 above, 27 to the left, 29 to the right and 32 below.
notes: Handy and Delavan lie on the edges of the sheet and are only partly drawn.
Livingston Avenue east of Comstock Street is not in the OpenStreetMap street network.
Livingston, Lee, Remsen Avenues, Comstock to Handy; Delavan left out (edge street).

sheet-29.description: Sheet 29 covers eight blocks in the south-western part of the city, in two rows of four, between Livingston Avenue at the top, Lee Avenue across the middle and Remsen Avenue at the bottom. The cross streets are, from left to right, Handy, Seaman, Suydam and Townsend, with another street cut off by the right edge. Blocks 180, 169, 160 and 149 lie north of Lee Avenue and blocks 179, 170, 159 and 150 south of it. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the grid turned about 51 degrees from north, and the compass rose stands at the top above block 160. The blocks are closely built with frame dwellings, mostly two or two and a half storeys, with stables, sheds and automobile garages in the rear lots. Corner stores and saloons stand on Remsen Avenue and Handy Street, and a store for rags is drawn in block 179. A garage stands in block 159 and an automobile supply shop with a gasoline tank in block 169. At the foot of Suydam Street, at the corner of Remsen Avenue in block 159, stands the fire department building of the Raritan Fire Company, with a note on its steam engine, hose wagon, chemical engine and volunteer members. Fire alarm boxes stand at Handy Street. Six-inch water pipes run in the streets, with twelve-inch mains under Livingston Avenue and eight-inch pipe under Remsen Avenue. Adjoining sheets are 23 and 24 above, 28 to the left, 30 to the right and 33 below.
notes: The street cut off by the right edge of the sheet could not be read; it is Redmond Street on sheet 30.
Livingston, Lee, Remsen Avenues, Handy to Townsend; one part.

sheet-30.description: Sheet 30 lies at the south-eastern end of the group of sheets 27 to 30. It has two parts side by side. At the left are two narrow blocks of closely built frame dwellings, 141 north and 140 south of Lee Avenue, bounded by Redmond Street at the left and Welton Street at the right, with Livingston Avenue above and Remsen Avenue below. At the right is one very large block, 132, bounded on the left by Welton Street, at the top by Livingston Avenue and at the lower right by George Street, with Morris Street curving from the top across the right side of the block. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, with the grid turned about 51 degrees from north. The Free Public Library, a brick building with a semicircular lecture hall, stands at the top of block 132, and the Livingston Avenue Baptist Church, heated by steam and lit by gas and electricity, in block 141. The Masonic Temple stands at the foot of block 140. J. M. Barkelew and Company, makers of aprons, have a factory with a stock room, a cutting room at the bottom of block 132, with a note on its watchman, heat and light. A garage, with a note on its power and supplies, and a row of dwellings face George Street at lower right. Most of block 132 is empty. Adjoining sheets are 24 above, 29 to the left and 34 below, and 25 to the right.
notes: Remsen Avenue east of Welton Street and Morris Street are not in the OpenStreetMap street network as drawn; the sheet is placed from the four junctions of Redmond and Welton with Lee and Remsen Avenues.
Livingston Avenue east of Comstock Street is not in the OpenStreetMap street network.
Redmond and Welton blocks, Free Public Library, Morris and George (curved, not used); 4 points.

sheet-31.description: Sheet 31 shows the Raritan River Railroad yard and the blocks south of Remsen Avenue in the south-western part of New Brunswick. Remsen Avenue forms the top of the sheet and Commercial Avenue the bottom, with Throop Avenue crossing the middle where it is interrupted by the lumber yard. The cross streets are, from left to right, Talmadge, Howard, Powers, Sandford and Delavan. The upper blocks are 256, 250, 237 and 230, the lower blocks 255, 251, 236 and 231. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the grid turned about 51 degrees from north. A fan of tracks of the Raritan River Railroad enters from the left across blocks 256 and 250 and runs to the right edge, with a freight shed and the company's passenger station beside them. The Howell Lumber Company yard occupies a large rectangle across the middle of the sheet with lumber piles of average height 7 and 10 feet, a lumber shed, a cement store and lime storage, and a tile store. The Crew Levick Oil Company tanks, two steel oil tanks and a gasoline tank, stand in block 250, and the Middlesex Hollow Block Building Block Company and Feigenspans' Brewery store house in block 237. The Public Service Street Railway Company car barn fills much of block 231. A repair shop and several frame dwellings stand in the lower blocks, and the New Brunswick Iron and Metal Company has a rags and paper store in block 230. Adjoining sheets are 27 above, 32 to the right and 36 below.
notes: Commercial Avenue is today Paul Robeson Boulevard.
Throop Avenue is covered by the lumber yard and the railroad tracks in the middle of the sheet.
Raritan River R.R. yard, Howell Lumber Co., Remsen to Commercial Avenue (Paul Robeson Boulevard), Talmadge to Delavan.

sheet-32.description: Sheet 32 covers eight blocks in the south-western part of New Brunswick, between Remsen Avenue at the top and Commercial Avenue at the bottom, with Throop Avenue running across the middle. The cross streets are, from left to right, Delavan, Comstock, Hale, Baldwin and Handy. The upper blocks are 217, 210, 197 and 190, the lower blocks 216 and 211 at left and the large City Park, blocks 196 and 191, at right. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 51 degrees from north, and the compass rose stands inside the park. Frame dwellings of two and two and a half storeys fill the street fronts, with a bakery, a tenement and a rag and paper store in block 197, and a saloon and a pool room at the corners. St. Mary of Mount Virgin Catholic Church, a brick building heated by stoves and lit by gas, stands at the top left in block 217. The Nathan Hale Public School, a brick building with hot air heat, fills the middle of block 211 on Comstock Street, and the Throop Avenue Mission stands on the Throop Avenue frontage of the same block. A bottler's premises, a wagon shed and a stable are drawn at the corner of Delavan Street and Throop Avenue. The park is left blank apart from its lettering. Water pipes of six, twelve and twenty inches run in the streets. Adjoining sheets are 28 above, 31 to the left, 33 to the right and 37 below.
notes: Commercial Avenue is today Paul Robeson Boulevard.
Remsen to Commercial Avenue, Delavan to Handy; City Park, Nathan Hale School.

sheet-33.description: Sheet 33 shows eight blocks of a residential district in the south-western part of New Brunswick, in two rows of four. Remsen Avenue forms the top of the sheet, Throop Avenue runs across the middle and Commercial Avenue closes the bottom. The cross streets, left to right, are Handy, Seaman, Suydam and Townsend, with Redmond cut by the right-hand edge. Blocks 178, 171, 158 and 151 lie in the upper row and blocks 177, 172, 157 and 152 in the lower. The fabric is mostly frame dwellings of two or two and a half storeys on narrow lots, with stables and sheds at the rear and a row of small buildings along the Throop Avenue frontage of the upper blocks. The main institution is the Church of the Sacred Heart (Roman Catholic), a large brick building with its convent beside it and the Sacred Heart School at the foot of the block, all around a cemetery that fills most of block 157 and carries the compass rose. Industrial uses are small: a greenhouse range in block 178, the F. A. Knoll cigar manufactory and the Central Cigar Factory, and the Roth Mfg. Co. Several lots in the lower row, notably most of block 177, are empty. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper right, so the street grid runs square to the page. Water pipes of 6 and 8 inches are marked in the streets and the 20-inch main appears under Commercial Avenue. Adjoining sheets are 29 above, 32 to the left, 34 and 39 to the right and 38 below.
notes: Commercial Avenue is today Paul Robeson Boulevard.
The cemetery in block 157 is lettered only as Cemetery, beside the Church of the Sacred Heart.
Remsen, Throop, Commercial Avenues, Handy to Redmond; one part.

sheet-34-1.description: Part 1 is the main map of sheet 34 and fills the right-hand and lower part of the page, outside the heavy-lined box at the upper left (part 2). It covers the district around George Street, a north-south street running down the page, in the western part of New Brunswick. Morris Street bounds the top, where a row of small frame dwellings fronts it, and Oliver Street crosses at about the middle with Hassart and Carman Streets below it and Throop Avenue at the foot. East of George Street the cross streets are Abeel and Neilson. The large block 120, between Morris and Oliver Streets, holds a cemetery with an old wagon shed and several outbuildings. Below Oliver Street the blocks are mostly frame dwellings, with the Pitman Methodist Church on the corner of George and Oliver, the Lord Sterling Public School on Abeel and Carman and the print-roller works of Burton and Richardson near Throop Avenue. At the left, Remsen Avenue curves in from the box and Welton Street runs diagonally down the page, so that blocks 133, 134 and 135 are drawn as wedges between them. The map is at 50 feet to an inch. The compass rose shows north towards the upper right, about 27 degrees from the vertical, which is a different orientation from the box. Water pipes of 4, 6, 8 and 20 inches run in the streets. Adjoining sheets are 26 above, 35 to the right, 39 below and 30 and 33 to the left.
notes: Oliver Street is probably today Tabernacle Way (George, Abeel and Neilson Streets meet it there); it is listed under that modern name for the control.
Neilson Street is drawn about 38 ft wide, narrower than the modern right-of-way.
The heavy line at the upper left separates this part from the box (part 2), which is drawn at another rotation.
Two parts: 1 main (George, Oliver, Hassart, rotation 25 deg; Neilson drawn 38 ft); 2 box upper left on the grid of sheet 33 (3 points, exact fit).

sheet-34-2.description: Part 2 is the box at the upper left of sheet 34, enclosed by a heavy double line that runs down the page and then diagonally to the left edge. It is drawn square to its own street grid, the same grid as sheet 33, so its north arrow points towards the upper right at a different angle from the main map. The box shows one row of blocks of frame dwellings between Remsen Avenue at the top and Throop Avenue at the bottom, west of Welton Street, with Redmond Street at the left edge. Block 139 holds the houses, with a boys' club (heated by stoves, no lights) among them and a few small stores at the Throop Avenue end. East of Welton Street the box is blank apart from the stubs of Hassart Street and Carman Street, which are lettered but not built up, and a row of unnumbered plots beside them. The scale is 50 feet to an inch. Six-inch water pipes run in Welton and Redmond Streets and 8-inch pipes in Remsen and Throop Avenues. The box continues the grid of sheet 33 to the west, and the main part of the sheet, which lies below and to the right of the heavy line, shows the same streets at a different rotation.
notes: Drawn square to the grid of sheet 33 (rotation about 51 degrees), unlike the main part of this sheet (about 25 degrees).
Georeferenced from three control points (an exact fit); its scale and rotation agree with sheets 33 and 37.
Two parts: 1 main (George, Oliver, Hassart, rotation 25 deg; Neilson drawn 38 ft); 2 box upper left on the grid of sheet 33 (3 points, exact fit).

sheet-35.description: Sheet 35 covers the district of New Brunswick between Richmond Street at the top and Oliver Street at the bottom, from Neilson Street on the left to the Delaware and Raritan Canal on the right. Burnet Street runs down the page near the middle of the right half, and John Street, New Street, Morris Street and Schureman Street cross the left half, several of them at an angle. The sheet is mixed in character. The upper left holds dense blocks of frame dwellings and small shops along Richmond, New and Schureman Streets, with the Joseph Hensler Brewing Co. and the Conrad Sebolt trucking stables in block 104. At the centre and bottom are lumber and woodworking plants: the Marine Mfg. and Supply Co. machine shop and foundry, H. V. Butler's sash, door and blind factory, the Builders Hardware Co. and Geo. B. Rule carpenter, and Mullen and Wendt's house finishing factory. A brook crosses the middle of the sheet, and the Fire Department Washington Engine Company house stands on Burnet Street. East of Burnet Street, along the canal, are coal and ice yards (John Collier Ice and Coal Co., Runyon Bros., T. C. Dugan), the Rolfe Building Material Co. lumber yard and other sheds and storage. A street at the top right is lettered Not Named. The map is at 50 feet to an inch and the compass rose, at the right, shows north towards the upper right. Adjoining sheets are 20 above, 26 and 34 to the left and 40 below.
notes: Oliver Street is probably today Tabernacle Way.
Burnet Street was largely replaced by Route 18 and Riverside Drive; the modern Burnet Street / Richmond Street node lies about 10 m from the drawn junction and was left out.
Morris Street east of Neilson Street is today Hildebrand Way, which curves away from the drawn line near John Street; the modern John Street / Hildebrand Way nodes were left out.
Schureman Street and the east end of New Street no longer exist.
One street at the top right is lettered Not Named.
Richmond to Oliver (Tabernacle Way), Neilson to the canal; heavily rebuilt (Route 18); 3 hand-picked points, low-medium confidence.

sheet-36.description: Sheet 36 shows the south-western edge of the built-up part of New Brunswick, between Commercial Avenue at the top and Nichol Avenue at the bottom. From left to right the cross streets are Talmadge, Howard, Powers, Sanford and Delavan, and Jones Avenue crosses the right-hand half. George's Road is drawn as a wide diagonal road running from the lower left up to the middle of the sheet, cutting off the wedge-shaped corner of block 235 and leaving a large undivided area, blocks 253 and 234, below it. Most of the sheet is empty lots. Frame dwellings stand along the north side, in blocks 254, 252 and 235, with a row of greenhouses in block 252 and a bowling alley on the Commercial Avenue frontage of block 235. In the centre of the lower half is the works of Reckitt's Ltd., blue manufacturers: concrete block buildings with a storage and press room, a tank, an accumulator house and automatic sprinklers, described in a note on the sheet. Block 232 at the right has a few dwellings, and block 233 has one. The map is at 50 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper right as shown by the compass rose at the lower left. Below the Nichol Avenue line a strip of another area carries a few buildings. Adjoining sheets are 31 above, 37 to the right and 40 and 41 below.
notes: Commercial Avenue is today Paul Robeson Boulevard.
Sanford Street is not in the OpenStreetMap extract and gave no control point.
George's Road is OpenStreetMap's Georges Road, where two ways run side by side.
Commercial, Jones, Nichol Avenues, Talmadge to Delavan; Rutgers Experimental Farm below Nichol.

sheet-37.description: Sheet 37 shows eight blocks of the south-western part of New Brunswick in two rows. Commercial Avenue forms the top, Jones Avenue crosses the middle and Nichol Avenue closes the bottom, and the streets running down the page are Delavan at the left, then Comstock, Hale and Baldwin, with Handy at the right edge. Blocks 215, 212, 195 and 192 lie in the upper row and blocks 214, 213, 194 and 193 in the lower. The upper blocks carry most of the buildings: a row of frame dwellings on narrow lots along the Commercial Avenue frontage of block 215, scattered dwellings in 212 and 195, and a saloon and boarding house with a wagon shed and a wood-sawing shop with a gasoline engine in the top right corner of block 212. The lower row is almost all empty land, with a handful of dwellings and a carpenter's shop. Below Nichol Avenue the sheet carries a strip belonging to the New Jersey Experimental Farm of Rutgers College Farm, showing hen houses and a lecture hall. A water main marked as supplied from the reservoir comes in from the bottom edge beside Comstock Street. The map is at 50 feet to an inch, and the compass rose in block 214 shows north towards the upper right. Adjoining sheets are 32 above, 36 to the left, 38 to the right and 42 below.
notes: Commercial Avenue is today Paul Robeson Boulevard.
The strip below Nichol Avenue is drawn within the sheet but is not part of the street grid fitted here.
Commercial, Jones, Nichol Avenues, Delavan to Handy; one part.

sheet-38.description: Sheet 38 covers eight blocks of the south-western edge of New Brunswick, laid out as two rows of four. Commercial Avenue forms the top, Jones Avenue crosses the middle and Nichol Avenue the bottom. The streets running down the page are Handy at the left, then Seaman, Suydam and Townsend, with Redmond at the right edge. The upper blocks, 176, 173, 156 and 153, have a few frame dwellings along the Commercial Avenue frontage, among them a junk yard in block 173, a painting shop and a small building marked with a letter C.B. in block 156, and a printing shop in block 153. Most of the sheet is unbuilt: blocks 175, 174 and 155 in the lower row are empty, and block 154 has only a few dwellings and a brick house with a stable. At the foot of the sheet, below the Nichol Avenue line, is the New Jersey Experimental Farm of Rutgers College Farm, with glass houses, a cement building and shed, a printing building and a laboratory, each lettered with its distance from the street. The map is at 50 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper right as shown by the compass rose at the lower left. Adjoining sheets are 33 above, 37 to the left, 39 to the right and 43 below.
notes: Commercial Avenue is today Paul Robeson Boulevard.
The farm buildings below Nichol Avenue are drawn within the sheet but are not part of the street grid fitted here.
Commercial, Jones, Nichol Avenues, Handy to Redmond; one part.

sheet-39.description: Sheet 39 covers a district of New Brunswick on both sides of Commercial Avenue, which crosses the sheet from left to right near its middle, with Throop Avenue along the top and Jones Avenue along the bottom. Redmond Street bounds the left side, George Street runs diagonally up the sheet from the bottom to the top centre, and Abeel and Neilson Streets run parallel to it on the right; Carman Street crosses the top right corner and Welton Street appears at the top left. Bishop Street crosses the lower part of the sheet, and a brook runs across the lower right beside it. Blocks 136, 124 and 123 north of Commercial Avenue are filled with two-storey frame dwellings on narrow lots with sheds and stables behind. Block 124 holds the Episcopal Church of St. John the Evangelist, and block 123 the Catholic Church of St. John the Baptist and the School of St. John the Baptist, drawn in the pink used for brick or stone. South of Commercial Avenue, block 110 has dwellings along Bishop Street with a tenement and a wagon shed, and block 137 holds a row of dwellings on George Street. Six-inch and larger water pipes run down the centre of the streets, with hydrants at most corners. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is turned so that north lies towards the upper right, as the compass at the right shows. Neilson Street is drawn much narrower than the other streets. Adjoining sheets are 33 and 38 at the left, 34 above, 40 to the right and 41 below.
notes: Commercial Avenue is today Paul Robeson Boulevard.
Neilson Street is drawn about 38 ft wide, against 67 to 84 ft of right-of-way today.
The modern George Street / Jones Avenue node lies about 20 m from the drawn junction and was not used.
Commercial / George / Neilson district to Bishop and Jones Avenue; one part.

sheet-40.description: Sheet 40 lies on the east side of New Brunswick, between Neilson Street at the left edge and Burnet Street, which runs down the right side of the built-up blocks beside the Delaware and Raritan Canal. Oliver, Hassart and Carman Streets cross the sheet from left to right at the top, middle and lower middle, and John Street runs down between Neilson and Burnet. Blocks 107, 108 and 109 are made up of lots of frame dwellings, with a bakery, a carpenter's shop, a wagon shed and a print shop; blocks 113, 114 and 112 at the left are similar, with a furniture ware house in block 114. At the top right the Cronk Mfg. Co., sash, doors and blinds, occupies the frontage on Burnet Street with a planing mill, a box factory, lumber sheds and a warehouse, and its notes on watchmen, power and fire pails are printed beside it. Blocks 103A and 103B east of Burnet Street are mostly open ground with a few dwellings, a sailmaking shop, a boat-building shed and an old building, running down to the canal bank, which is drawn with a sinuous outline. Commercial Avenue crosses the lower left diagonally past a brook and the United Cigar Mfrs. Co. tobacco stripping house in block 110, and Bishop Street meets Burnet Street at the bottom. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper right, and the compass is at the right. Adjoining sheets are 34 and 39 at the left, 35 above and 41 below.
notes: Oliver Street is probably today's Tabernacle Way; the spacing along Neilson Street agrees to within 4 percent.
Hassart and Carman Streets are drawn through to Burnet Street; the modern streets end at Neilson Street.
Commercial Avenue is today Paul Robeson Boulevard.
Burnet Street, John Street and the Oliver Street line were rebuilt with Route 18, so the modern nodes may not follow the 1912 lines.
Neilson to Burnet Street and the D&R Canal; Cronk Mfg Co.; 3 hand-picked T-junctions; low-medium confidence.

sheet-41-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 41 shows Burnet Street running south-east from Bishop Street along the Delaware and Raritan Canal and the Raritan River, at the south-eastern edge of the city below sheets 39 and 40. At the top, between Bishop Street and the canal, stands the works of the Emerson Contracting Company: a long brick machine shop, boiler shop and sheet metal working shop, storage and wash room, under a watchman with a six-station clock. Next to it Thomas Lea's machine shop and auto repairing shop occupies a small brick building with an office. Along Burnet Street below are rows of two-storey frame dwellings, a cobbler, stables, sheds and two small buildings marked as canal property and private. Further south the east side of Burnet Street is open ground marked as the top of a high bluff, with the Elizabeth Wray Memorial Chapel at its upper end and only a few scattered dwellings below; the canal and the river bank run down the right of the sheet. The left of the part is blank and belongs to sheet 39; the dash-dot match line A to B there repeats the one drawn on sheet 39. Drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north to the upper right, turned about 11 degrees from sheet 39; a heavy line separates it from part 2, the river bank further down stream.
notes: Burnet Street along the river is now Route 18; no junction on the part survives. Placed from the match-line corners A and B carried from sheet 39 (A as the anchor, B 1.9 m from the anchored fit), at the configured scale and a north direction of 40 degrees; low confidence.

Burnet Street along the Raritan River and D&R Canal south-east of Bishop Street; two parts divided by a heavy line. Part 1 placed from match-line corners A and B carried from sheet 39 (low confidence); part 2 (river bank further down stream: Canal hen house, old repair shop, hotel) unplaced.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: Burnet Street and the river bank further down stream (lower left) (no surviving street junction (Route 18); needs hand-picked parcel corners).

sheet-42-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 42 is the main map of the sheet, showing a strip of Highland Park north of the Raritan River. Highland Avenue runs along the top, and the cross streets run down the page: Cleveland Avenue at the left edge, then Harrison, Grant and Lincoln Avenues, with Lawrence Avenue crossing the sheet diagonally from the lower centre to the right edge. River Road is lettered at the bottom left, and Rutgers Place forms a small curved street on the south side of Lawrence Avenue. A street lettered Grant Avenue also runs across the bottom between Harrison and Lawrence. The large block 1A at the left is almost empty, with a few dwellings and auto houses, while blocks 2A and 3A between Harrison and Lincoln Avenues carry two rows of two-storey frame dwellings, most labelled plastered or wire lath and plaster, and block 2A includes a foundation outline. At the right a block of playgrounds fills the angle between Lincoln and Lawrence Avenues. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes with hydrants run down the streets. The part is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is turned, with north towards the upper left according to the compass near Rutgers Place. A separately framed inset, drawn with north at the top, fills the lower right corner and is not included in this part. Adjoining sheets are 43 and 44 above, 45 to the right and below, and 46 beyond the right edge.
notes: Highland Avenue is today North 2nd Avenue.
The street printed Grant Av. along the bottom, between Harrison Avenue and the diagonal Lawrence Avenue, is modern Lawrence Avenue west of Grant Avenue.
The Harrison Avenue / River Road junction lies just below the bottom edge of the sheet.
Highland Park. Two parts: 1 main (Highland Avenue = North 2nd Avenue, Harrison, Grant, Lincoln, Lawrence, River Road); 2 inset lower right (Cedar Avenue and a pond), unplaced.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Cedar Avenue and a pond (no street junction; needs hand-picked parcel corners or the Cedar Avenue line (step 6b)).

sheet-43.description: Sheet 43 is dominated by the wall paper printing works of Janeway and Carpenter, which fill the centre of the sheet between Cleveland Avenue on the right and the Pennsylvania Railroad on the left. The works are drawn in the pink used for mill construction and consist of a long store house and a manufacturing building with a central yard, an office, colour building, mixing room and printing rooms at the south end, an engine house, a reservoir and a water tank beside Cleveland Avenue, with sprinklers, hydrants and a watchman's clock system described in notes below the buildings. Madison Avenue crosses the top of the sheet and Highland Avenue the bottom, with a street lettered Janeway running from Cleveland Avenue towards the railroad south of the works. East of Cleveland Avenue, between it and Harrison Avenue, are Livingston Manor Corporation's builders' storage and its builders' finish factory, the Crittenden Printing Co., the Highland Park Dairy, a plumber's shop, wagon sheds, a milk depot and a few dwellings. At the lower left a cement storage building and a coal shed stand beside the railroad, which curves down the left side of the sheet. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper left, as the compass at the top left shows. Adjoining sheets are 42 below and 44 to the right.
notes: Highland Avenue is today North 2nd Avenue.
Janeway is today Janeway Avenue.
Harrison Avenue junctions with North 2nd Avenue and Madison Avenue were hand-picked.
Highland Park: Janeway & Carpenter wall paper works, Cleveland and Madison Avenues; 2 hand-picked points.

sheet-44.description: Sheet 44 shows the part of Highland Park lying north of Highland Avenue, in four columns of blocks separated by Harrison, Grant, Lincoln and Lawrence Avenues, which run down the page, and crossed by Madison Avenue at the top, a street lettered Court across the middle and Highland Avenue at the bottom. The upper tier of blocks, numbered 1A, 2A and 3A, and the tier below them are largely empty ground with the block numbers printed in them; the lower tier, between Court and Highland Avenue, holds the dwellings. Block 8A at the left is marked as scattered lumber piles with a print shop and a few buildings, block 7A and block 6A carry rows of two-storey frame dwellings facing Grant and Lincoln Avenues, and the narrow lots of block 5A face Lawrence Avenue. At the right a street lettered 3rd Av. crosses above a block with a compass, Wayne Street runs diagonally down the right side, and 2nd Av. appears at the bottom right. The top right corner carries more dwellings and a hen house on block 4A. Six-inch water pipes run down the avenues. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper left, following the compass at the right. Adjoining sheets are 43 at the left, 42 below, and 46 and 47 at the right.
notes: Highland Avenue is today North 2nd Avenue.
The street printed 3rd Av., and the Court row beside it, is modern North 3rd Avenue; the junction with Lawrence Avenue agrees with the fit to 0.7 m.
2nd Av. at the bottom right is North 2nd Avenue.
Highland Park blocks between Madison and Highland Avenue (North 2nd Avenue); one part.

sheet-45.description: Sheet 45 covers the riverside corner of Highland Park where River Road, Lawrence Avenue, Lincoln Avenue and Raritan Avenue meet at the Raritan River, which runs down the left side of the sheet. River Road runs diagonally from the top left to the bottom and meets Raritan Avenue, which crosses the bottom of the sheet and becomes a bridge over the river at the left. Harrison and Grant Avenues run in from the top and meet Lawrence Avenue, which crosses the upper part of the sheet to the right edge, with Parkway running parallel to it below. Rutgers Place curves down the right side from Lawrence Avenue to Raritan Avenue, and Adelaide Avenue runs down at the right edge, joined to Rutgers Place by a curved street. The ground is mostly large open lots with only a few buildings: dwellings along Lawrence Avenue and River Road, a tobacco store house and wagon shed beside Rutgers Place, the Airdome open air theatre and a steam laundry with an auto house on River Road, a cement shed, and a transformer house near the bridge.
