A ten inch supply main from New Brunswick crosses the sheet to the river. At the top left an area marked to be a playground and boat club is drawn on the river bank. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is turned slightly, with north a little to the right of the top according to the compass at the left. Adjoining sheets are 42 above, 46 to the right and 48 below.
notes: Rutgers Place is today the south part of Lincoln Avenue, from Raritan Avenue to the curve of North Adelaide Avenue.
Adelaide Avenue is drawn as two offset streets at Raritan Avenue; the modern node is one.
The modern Grant Avenue / Lawrence Avenue node lies about 30 m from the drawn junction and was not used.
Highland Park: Raritan River corner, River Road, Rutgers Place (= Lincoln Avenue), Raritan Avenue; Grant Avenue left out (modern node about 30 m off).

sheet-46.description: Sheet 46 lies at the west end of the borough of Highland Park, on the north side of the Raritan River district, and is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned so that north lies to the left and Raritan Avenue runs up the right-hand side of the page. Raritan Avenue is the main street, with the lots numbered 311 to 318 fronting it on the west side and Adelaide Avenue crossing it near the bottom with a small jog between its two halves. 1st Avenue and a short Cedar Street open off the east side. In the upper left a parkway and Lawrence Avenue curve around the edge of a large blank tract, and at the lower left Lawrence Avenue ends at a drawn oval, a traffic circle or park, beside Rutgers Place, which runs diagonally to the bottom edge. The Berger and Fischer Brewery fills the upper middle of the sheet, with an ice house, freezing tank, cooling house, grain storage, wash house, brew house and bottling and storage buildings, and an open lot beside it facing Brewery Lane; its card notes steam heat and power, electric light, and a well and city water supply. The Johnson and Johnson plaster and fumigator factory stands at the bottom near Rutgers Place, with an adhesive plaster factory, sulphur mixing house, grease rendering house and a formaldehyde torch packing shed. A row of small dwellings, mostly stuccoed frame, stands along Lawrence Avenue and a few detached houses stand along Raritan Avenue. Most of the interior is vacant ground. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes are marked in the streets. Adjoining sheets are 44 and 42 on the left, 47 above, 51 and 48 on the right and 45 below.
notes: Raritan Avenue is the modern Raritan Avenue; Adelaide Avenue is modern North Adelaide Avenue (left of Raritan Avenue) and South Adelaide Avenue (right).
1st Avenue is modern South 1st Avenue.
Rutgers Place roughly follows the modern Lincoln Avenue; its modern line was not used as control.
Cedar Street and Parkway do not appear in the modern OpenStreetMap street network under these names.
Georeferenced from only two junctions on Raritan Avenue, so the placement rests on a helmert fit through two points on one street.
Highland Park west end, turned (north to the left); only Raritan Avenue junctions with South Adelaide and South 1st Avenue; helmert, low confidence.

sheet-47.description: Sheet 47 covers a strip of the western part of Highland Park north of Raritan Avenue, which runs along the bottom of the page. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the top, the grid turned about 25 degrees from the page. Three streets run up the sheet, Brewery Lane on the left, 2nd Avenue in the middle and 3rd Avenue at the right edge, and are crossed by Denison, Montgomery and Wayne streets, each marked 60 feet wide. 2nd Avenue is marked 80 feet wide and 3rd Avenue 80 feet below Denison; at the top left 2nd Avenue turns north-west and is lettered Highland Av., meeting Lawrence Av. and a Parkway that leads off to the left past a triangular block. Most of the blocks are large and nearly empty, numbered as lots 2A, 3A, 4A and 5A, with a scatter of small dwellings, outbuildings and sheds along their edges, a tin-clad double house on Montgomery Street and a row of five dwellings along 3rd Avenue. The built-up frontage is along Raritan Avenue at the bottom, where the Highland Park Baptist Church (heated by steam, lit by electricity), a carpenter shop with a gas engine and a row of detached frame dwellings face the street. At the lower left the Fire Department's Highland Park Hose Company stands at the corner of Brewery Lane and Raritan Avenue; its card lists a volunteer company of sixty-five men, a hose wagon, hand chemical extinguishers and ladders. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes are marked in the streets, with a drinking hydrant at the right edge. Adjoining sheets are 46 on the left, 44 above, 48 on the right and 51 and 52 below.
notes: 2nd Avenue and 3rd Avenue here are modern North 2nd Avenue and North 3rd Avenue, north of Raritan Avenue.
Wayne, Montgomery and Denison are printed without a street suffix; the modern names are Wayne Street, Montgomery Street and Denison Street.
Highland Av. at the top left continues the line of modern North 2nd Avenue north-west; modern Highland Avenue is elsewhere in the borough.
Brewery Lane and Parkway do not appear in the modern OpenStreetMap street network under these names.
Highland Park: North 2nd / 3rd Avenue, Wayne, Montgomery, Denison, Raritan; one part.

sheet-48-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 48 is the left-hand strip of the sheet, the district of Highland Park north of Raritan Avenue between 3rd Avenue at the left edge and 4th Avenue at the heavy dividing line on the right. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper right, the grid turned about 25 degrees from the page. Wayne, Montgomery and Denison streets cross it from side to side, each marked 60 feet wide, and Raritan Avenue runs along the bottom, with the end of a block of detached dwellings fronting it. The blocks are large and mostly open, numbered as lots 1A, 2A and 3A, with a scatter of small frame dwellings, hen houses and stables. At the left, beside 3rd Avenue, the Pembroke Process Company, manufacturers of typewriter ribbons, has a small frame works with an engine room; its card records no watchman, power from a 3 horsepower gasoline engine, stoves and kerosene lamps for heat and light, and no fire apparatus. A row of about nine detached houses stands along the north side of Raritan Avenue at the bottom. A compass rose in the middle block shows north to the upper right. The strip is separated from the right-hand part of the sheet by a heavy double line; 4th Avenue lies along it and the printed 'Highland Park' title straddles it near the top. Six-inch and two-inch water pipes are marked in the streets, with hydrants at the corners. Adjoining sheets are 47 on the left, 45 and 49 above and to the right, and 52 below.
notes: 3rd Avenue and 4th Avenue here are modern North 3rd Avenue and North 4th Avenue; Wayne, Montgomery and Denison are printed without a suffix (modern Wayne Street, Montgomery Street, Denison Street).
The mask follows the centre of the heavy dividing line, which runs through the carriageway of 4th Avenue.
Highland Park, two parts: 1 left strip (North 3rd / 4th Avenue); 2 right strip south of Raritan (South Adelaide, Cedar), anchored, low confidence.

sheet-48-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 48 is the right-hand part of the sheet, a strip of Highland Park south of Raritan Avenue, which runs along the top of the page. It is separated from part 1 by a heavy double line and has its own north arrow, pointing slightly right of the top of the page; the sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Adelaide Avenue runs down the page near the left and Cedar Street along the right-hand edge. Between the dividing line and Adelaide Avenue is a long narrow block, numbered 4A and 0, holding a few frame dwellings, a small pink building marked tile, and sheds, and the rest left open. The block between Adelaide Avenue and Cedar Street is divided into narrow numbered lots (101 to 122, with lots lettered along the left side), mostly detached frame dwellings with stables and hen houses. The E. M. Uniack Manufacturing Company, lamp and brass manufacturers, occupies a brick-and-frame works on the Cedar Street side, with storage and packing on the first floor and finishing on the second; its card notes steam heat, 5 horsepower, an electric motor, electric lights, fire buckets throughout and no watchman. Further south on Cedar Street two large square outbuildings stand behind the lots. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes are marked in all the streets, with hydrants at several points. The bottom of the part carries the scale bar and library stamp. Adjoining sheets are 46 above to the left, 51 to the right and 45 and 49 below.
notes: Adelaide Avenue here is modern South Adelaide Avenue, south of Raritan Avenue.
Cedar is printed without a suffix and does not appear as a street in the modern OpenStreetMap network; sheet 46 prints it as Cedar St.
Georeferenced from a single junction (Raritan Avenue and Adelaide Avenue at the top of the part) at the atlas scale; low confidence.
Highland Park, two parts: 1 left strip (North 3rd / 4th Avenue); 2 right strip south of Raritan (South Adelaide, Cedar), anchored, low confidence.

sheet-49.description: Sheet 49 covers part of Highland Park north of Raritan Avenue, which runs along the bottom of the page, between 4th Avenue on the left and the long diagonal line of 5th Avenue on the right. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper right, the grid turned about 25 degrees from the page, and a compass rose at the right edge shows this. Montgomery and Denison streets run across the left half, each marked 60 feet wide, and Mill Road cuts diagonally from Montgomery Street at the upper left to meet 5th Avenue, marked 40 feet wide. 5th Avenue is marked 70 feet near the bottom and 50 feet at the top. Abbott Avenue opens off the right side of 5th Avenue near the top. The blocks are large and thinly built: a triangular block between 4th Avenue and Mill Road holds a single dwelling, and the block between Mill Road and Denison Street has a row of about ten frame dwellings along its lower edge, a few outbuildings and a stable. South of Denison Street a long block, numbered 4A, runs down to Raritan Avenue with a scatter of two-storey frame dwellings, hen houses and sheds, divided into narrow lots near the bottom. A group of small frame buildings and sheds stands on the north side of Mill Road beside 5th Avenue. The top of the sheet is marked no exposure and a strip of blocks at the bottom edge belongs to sheet 52. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes run in the streets, with hydrants at corners. Adjoining sheets are 48 on the left, 50 on the right and 52 below.
notes: 4th Avenue and 5th Avenue here are modern North 4th Avenue and North 5th Avenue; Abbott Avenue is modern Abbott Street; Montgomery and Denison are printed without a suffix (modern Montgomery Street, Denison Street).
Mill Road is not in the modern OpenStreetMap network under that name; the modern Montgomery Street follows the line of the drawn Mill Road to 5th Avenue.
The fitted scale is about 1 percent below the other Highland Park sheets and leave-one-out is about 3 m, so the fit is medium confidence.
Highland Park: North 4th / 5th Avenue, Mill Road (Montgomery Street), Abbott; one part.

sheet-50.description: Sheet 50 shows the central part of Highland Park north of Raritan Avenue, where the avenue bends and runs diagonally across the lower part of the page. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the grid turned about 10 degrees from the page, and a compass rose at the upper left shows north towards the top. Four long avenues run up the sheet, 5th Avenue at the left edge, then 6th, 7th and 8th, crossed near the top by Abbott Avenue, and the blocks between them are numbered 1A to 8A. Mill Road and Denison Street end at the left edge against 5th Avenue. Raritan Avenue meets Woodbridge Avenue at a fork near the lower middle: Raritan Avenue runs off to the upper right, Woodbridge Avenue continues along the bottom of the page, and a long wedge-shaped lot between them holds the Highland Park Inn, a two-and-a-half storey frame hotel heated by hot water and lit by electricity, with sheds and dwellings around it. Most of the blocks are open ground. The only close building is a row of dwellings along 7th Avenue in block 6A and three pairs of two-storey houses on 6th and 7th Avenues in block 7A, with a row of small dwellings and a small pink building marked tile in the lower left corner of block 8A beside 5th Avenue. Block 10A at the bottom is marked vacant. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes are marked in the streets and hydrants stand at several corners. The street widths are given as 60, 70 and 100 feet. Sheet 49 adjoins on the left.
notes: 5th Avenue to 8th Avenue here are modern North 5th Avenue to North 8th Avenue; Abbott Avenue is modern Abbott Street.
Mill Road is not in the modern OpenStreetMap network under that name; the modern Montgomery Street follows its line.
North 8th Avenue does not reach Raritan Avenue in the modern network where the sheet draws it, so that junction was left out of the control.
Highland Park: North 5th to 8th Avenue, Abbott, Raritan / Woodbridge fork; North 8th / Raritan excluded.

sheet-51.description: Sheet 51 covers the part of Highland Park south of Raritan Avenue between Cedar Street at the left edge and 2nd Avenue near the right, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper right (the grid is turned about 17 degrees) and a compass rose at the right. Raritan Avenue runs slantwise along the top. 1st Avenue and 2nd Avenue run down the page and are crossed by Park Place, Magnolia Street and Benner Street, with Johnson Street along the bottom edge. The block on Raritan Avenue at the top left, numbered 6 on the Cedar Street side, is the only one with business frontage: a drug store, a pool room and tailor, a bakery, stores and a wagon shed stand at the corner, beside a row of dwellings along the street. The lots on Raritan Avenue are numbered 323 to 337. Elsewhere the sheet is residential, mostly detached two and two-and-a-half storey frame houses with stables and sheds, the lots lettered along the rear lines and numbered 204 to 206 and 401 to 425 along the streets. Block 5 and block 2A contain the largest lots, with scattered houses; block 4 at the upper right is open ground with a compass rose beside it. Lots in the lower left block, 1A, include two pink brick buildings and sheds. Six-inch water pipes run in each street, with hydrants at several corners. Brewery Lane appears at the top edge where sheet 47 meets Raritan Avenue. Adjoining sheets are 48 on the left, 46 and 47 above, 52 on the right.
notes: 1st Avenue and 2nd Avenue here are modern South 1st Avenue and South 2nd Avenue; Magnolia, Benner and Johnson are printed without a suffix (modern Magnolia Street, Benner Street, Johnson Street).
Park Place was left out of the control because its modern junction with 1st Avenue was 2.5 m off the drawn one.
Cedar is half drawn at the left edge and was not used as control.
Highland Park south of Raritan: South 1st / 2nd Avenue, Magnolia, Benner, Johnson; Park Place left out.

sheet-52.description: Sheet 52 covers the south-eastern part of the Highland Park map, south of Raritan Avenue, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the sheet turned so that north lies towards the left and Raritan Avenue runs up the left side of the page. The avenues numbered 4th, 3rd and 2nd run across it from top to bottom, 3rd Avenue marked 80 feet wide, and Magnolia and Benner streets run down the page and cut them into large blocks. A compass rose in the block at the upper left shows north to the left. The upper left block, numbered 1A, holds a row of narrow lots lettered A to G with small frame dwellings, a bakery building in pink beside the compass rose and further dwellings below. The long block between Raritan Avenue and Magnolia Street at the lower left, numbered 9, has a close row of detached dwellings along Raritan Avenue, lots numbered in the 300s, and several works and institutions: J. S. Turner's white metal works, with a machine shop, melting pot, engine room and asbestos-covered brick-chimney building, heated and powered by steam with electric light and no watchman; the Highland Park Reformed Church, a brick church with a tower, heated by steam and lit by electricity; and its Sunday school. The block between Magnolia and Benner streets, numbered 5A, is mostly open ground with a few houses and a printing shop of stucco. The Highland Park School, drawn in pink at the lower right, is a large frame school heated by furnace and lit by gas and electricity. The right edge carries more houses along Benner Street. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes are marked in the streets. Adjoining sheets are 49 above, 47 and 48 on the left and 51 below.
notes: 2nd, 3rd and 4th Avenue here are modern South 2nd Avenue, South 3rd Avenue and South 4th Avenue; Magnolia and Benner are printed without a suffix (modern Magnolia Street and Benner Street).
South 2nd Avenue is set to 50 feet wide for the detector, narrower than the parcels, because the drawn street is cut by the bottom edge of the sheet.
The fitted scale is about 3 percent below the other Highland Park sheets, so the sheet may be drawn slightly under scale.
Highland Park south of Raritan, turned (north to the left): South 2nd to 4th Avenue, Magnolia, Benner.

sheet-53-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 53 is the industrial strip along the west side of the Pennsylvania Railroad between Jersey Avenue and the tracks, from Sandford Street at the top of the sheet southwards past Talmadge Street, at the south-western edge of New Brunswick near Mile Run. Nearly all of it is occupied by works. At the top, block 242 holds the Johnson and Johnson Corporation box shop and related buildings, with lumber piles and a railroad siding curving in from the main line, and a large reinforced concrete building being built and to be occupied by the Simplex Automobile Company. Block 245 below is the Empire Foundry Company: foundry, machine shop, pattern and assembling shops, core room, cupola and engine room, much of it marked as used by Simplex. Further down, block 261 is mostly open, with the Standard Oil Company's warehouse near Jersey Avenue above Talmadge Street. Below Talmadge, block 264 holds the Brunswick Refrigerating Company, with an office, several works buildings and lumber piles. The sidings and main tracks of the railroad run down the right side of the part to the heavy dividing line. Water pipes of 8 and 12 inches run in Jersey Avenue and Sandford Street. Drawn at 50 feet to an inch with Jersey Avenue running up the page; north is to the upper left.
notes: Placed from one hand-checked junction, Jersey Avenue / Sandford Street, at the configured scale with rotation from the measured street lines; low confidence.
Talmadge Street no longer reaches Jersey Avenue in OpenStreetMap; the Johnson and Johnson site covers it.

Three parts divided by heavy lines: 1 Jersey Avenue south of Sandford Street (Johnson & Johnson, Empire Foundry, Brunswick Refrigerating); 2 the wedge between Commercial Avenue (Paul Robeson Boulevard) and Georges Road (Evergreen Cemetery, New Brunswick Coal & Ice Co., trolley right of way); 3 Georges Road further out (National Musical String Co.). Only part 1 placed.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: Commercial Avenue (Paul Robeson Boulevard) and Georges Road: Evergreen Cemetery, New Brunswick Coal & Ice Co., Middlesex Granite & Marble Works (no junction of surviving streets drawn in the part; needs hand-picked parcel corners or street-line control along Paul Robeson Boulevard and Georges Road).

Not georeferenced on this sheet: Georges Road near the Raritan River Railroad: National Musical String Co. (no street junction; the Raritan River Railroad is not in OpenStreetMap; needs hand-picked parcel corners along Georges Road).

sheet-54-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 54 shows the western edge of the city where Somerset Street and French Street cross Mile Run Brook, west of the blocks on sheet 14. Somerset Street runs diagonally across the top of the part and French Street along the bottom, with Sandford Street meeting French at the lower right. Between them is a thinly built tract with a scatter of two-storey frame dwellings along Somerset, sheds, a large brick building marked as a rubber factory being built at the left, and brick tenements near French Street on both sides of the brook. S. Lederer and Son's fertilizer works, with grinding and storage buildings and a watchman, stands beside Mile Run Brook near Somerset Street. A cemetery is lettered along the south side of French Street at the bottom of the part. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches run in French and Sandford streets. Drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north to the upper right; a heavy line separates it from Riverside Park to the left and from the Landing Road area below.
notes: Placed from one hand-picked junction, French Street / Sandford Street, at the configured scale and a north direction of 16 degrees read from the street lines; low confidence.

Four specials parts divided by heavy lines: 1 Riverside Park (3/4 mile N of the court house: dance hall, summer theatre) on the Raritan River; 2 Somerset and French Streets at Mile Run Brook (Lederer fertilizer works); 3 John Waldron Machine Works, Highland Park, on the Pennsylvania Railroad; 4 George Street and Landing Road at the canal. Parts 2 and 4 placed from one hand-picked junction each.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: Riverside Park, 3/4 mile north of the court house: dance hall, summer theatre (no street drawn; only the river bank).

Not georeferenced on this sheet: John Waldron Machine Works, Highland Park, beside the Pennsylvania Railroad (no street junction or rail crossing drawn; needs hand-picked parcel corners or carried points from sheet 43).

sheet-54-4.description: Part 4 of sheet 54 shows the north-western end of George Street where Landing Road leaves it, beside the Delaware and Raritan Canal, at the northern edge of New Brunswick near the Landing Bridge over the Raritan River. The canal and its swing bridge run along the top of the part, George Street, 40 feet wide, below it, and Landing Road, 32 feet wide, runs from George Street down the page to the bottom edge. The area is almost open: a shed and a dwelling on George Street, a group of frame dwellings and an automobile garage to the right, a larger dwelling with outbuildings lower down, and a few small buildings along Landing Road near the bottom of the sheet. Drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north nearly straight up; a heavy line separates it from the John Waldron machine works in Highland Park to the left.
notes: Landing Road is today Landing Lane.

Placed from one hand-picked junction, George Street / Landing Lane, at the configured scale and a north direction of -8 degrees from the line of George Street; low confidence (Landing Lane has been rebuilt).

Four specials parts divided by heavy lines: 1 Riverside Park (3/4 mile N of the court house: dance hall, summer theatre) on the Raritan River; 2 Somerset and French Streets at Mile Run Brook (Lederer fertilizer works); 3 John Waldron Machine Works, Highland Park, on the Pennsylvania Railroad; 4 George Street and Landing Road at the canal. Parts 2 and 4 placed from one hand-picked junction each.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: Riverside Park, 3/4 mile north of the court house: dance hall, summer theatre (no street drawn; only the river bank).

Not georeferenced on this sheet: John Waldron Machine Works, Highland Park, beside the Pennsylvania Railroad (no street junction or rail crossing drawn; needs hand-picked parcel corners or carried points from sheet 43).

sheet-9999997.description: The Map of Congested District of New Brunswick, dated 1912 and drawn at 200 feet to an inch, is a single preliminary sheet covering the whole built-up centre of the city on one page, with the large grey numbers of the 50-foot sheets (2 to 41) printed over the areas they cover. It reaches from Central Avenue, Mine and Hamilton streets and Rutgers College at the top to Livingston Avenue, Codwise Avenue, Remsen and Throop at the bottom, and from the Baldwin, Handy and Seaman grid on the left to the Raritan River and the Delaware and Raritan Canal on the right. The Pennsylvania Railroad crosses the sheet diagonally from lower left to upper right on its embankment, with Wall Street and Railroad Avenue beside it. The commercial core along George, Albany, Church, Neilson, Dennis, Hiram, Burnet and Peace streets is drawn densely in pink brick, with fire department houses in black; the residential districts around it are mostly yellow frame dwellings. Rutgers College grounds, the seminary on College Avenue and the factory district along the canal and Burnet Street are shown. Street widths are lettered in feet and the grey lines in George, Albany, Somerset, Easton Avenue, Livingston Avenue and other streets are street car tracks. Streets are drawn wider than to scale at this reduction. The sheet repeats in outline what sheets 2 to 41 show at 50 feet to an inch and adds nothing outside them; in the assembled atlas it lies under those sheets.
notes: Scale 200 ft to an inch; the scan is of a larger sheet than the 50 ft sheets, so its fitted px_per_ft (about 2.0) is about a quarter of theirs.
Neilson Street was left out of the fit: its junctions came out 3 to 7 m off, measured from edges drawn about 40 ft apart against 65 to 85 ft parcels.
Codwise Avenue is today Joyce Kilmer Avenue; Commercial Avenue is Paul Robeson Boulevard.
Street name list is not exhaustive: names read on half-scale crops and the overview only.

Preliminary sheet: Map of congested district of New Brunswick, 1912, scale 200 ft to an inch; downtown from College Avenue and the Pennsylvania Railroad to the Raritan River and Delaware and Raritan Canal. Repeats sheets at 50 ft; one part.
